title: Persian-Style Kuku Sabzi with Walnuts & Barberries
dek: A deep-green, herb-packed Persian egg cake bakes up tender beneath a burnished crust, with toasted walnuts and tart barberries adding the exact crunch and jewel-bright finish shown in every wedge.
image_alt: Triangular wedge of dark-green Persian kuku sabzi topped with walnut halves and red barberries on a white plate
ingredients: 1 packed cup flat-leaf parsley leaves and tender stems, washed and dried completely
1 packed cup cilantro leaves and tender stems, washed and dried completely
1 packed cup fresh dill fronds, washed and dried completely
1 packed cup chives, cut into 1-inch lengths
1 packed cup scallion greens, cut into 1-inch lengths
1/2 cup walnut pieces, toasted and cooled, divided
1/3 cup dried barberries, picked over, rinsed and dried, divided
1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt, for serving
1 cup mixed radishes and cucumber slices, for serving

instructions.name: Heat the oven and prepare the skillet
instructions.text: Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat to 350°F. Brush the bottom and sides of a 10-inch oven-safe nonstick or well-seasoned skillet with 1 tablespoon olive oil. Set the remaining oil beside the stove; the egg mixture should go into a hot, freshly oiled pan as soon as it is mixed.

instructions.name: Dry and finely chop the herbs
instructions.text: Spin the parsley, cilantro, dill, chives and scallion greens completely dry, then blot any damp spots with a clean towel. Working in four batches, pulse the herbs in a food processor 6 to 8 times until finely chopped but not wet or puréed. Measure 5 packed cups; if chopping by hand, use a sharp knife and stop before the herbs release a puddle of green liquid.

instructions.name: Whisk the seasoned egg base
instructions.text: In a large bowl, whisk the eggs until the whites and yolks are fully blended. Sprinkle the flour, baking powder, turmeric, salt and black pepper evenly over the surface and whisk until no flour pockets remain. Fold in the chopped herbs, 1/3 cup walnuts and 1/4 cup barberries. The mixture will look far more like herbs coated with egg than a conventional frittata batter.

instructions.name: Set the bottom crust on the stove
instructions.text: Heat the prepared skillet over medium for 90 seconds. Add the remaining 2 tablespoons olive oil and swirl to coat. Scrape in the herb mixture, spread it level without packing it down and cook undisturbed for 4 minutes, until the edge bubbles gently and a thin set rim appears. Reduce the heat if the oil smokes or the herbs at the edge blacken.

instructions.name: Bake until safely set
instructions.text: Transfer the skillet to the 350°F oven and bake for 18 to 22 minutes. Begin checking at 18 minutes: the center should be firm to a light press, a thin knife should come out without liquid egg and a thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°F. Do not wait for the center to brown; the surface stays deep green while the underside and rim become golden.

instructions.name: Broil briefly for a burnished top
instructions.text: Switch the oven to broil and move the skillet about 6 inches from the element for 1 to 2 minutes, watching continuously, until the high spots are lightly bronzed. Remove the skillet with a dry oven mitt and immediately cover the hot handle with a second mitt or handle sleeve so no one grabs it. Rest for 8 minutes.

instructions.name: Release and garnish to match the finished dish
instructions.text: Run a thin silicone spatula around the edge, invert the kuku onto a plate, then invert again onto a serving platter so the green top faces up. Press the remaining walnut pieces and barberries lightly into the surface while it is warm. Cut into 6 triangular wedges with a serrated knife, wiping the blade between cuts.

instructions.name: Serve warm or at room temperature
instructions.text: Serve one wedge per person with yogurt, warm flatbread, radishes and cucumber. Kuku sabzi is equally useful at room temperature, but do not leave it out longer than 2 hours total. For a smaller appetizer portion, cut each wedge in half after the kuku has cooled enough to hold a clean edge.

why_it_works: Five packed cups of finely chopped herbs to eight eggs produce kuku sabzi's dense green structure instead of the pale, custardy interior of a standard frittata.
Thoroughly drying the herbs prevents their surface water from steaming the egg cake and weakening the browned bottom crust.
Flour absorbs stray herb moisture while baking powder provides just enough lift to keep the tall herb layer tender rather than compressed.
Starting in a hot, oiled skillet sets a sturdy base for clean wedges; finishing in the oven cooks the thick center evenly without a risky stovetop flip.
Holding back part of the toasted walnuts and barberries preserves crispness and creates the visible red-and-gold garnish in the licensed finished-dish photograph.
swaps: Use 1 tablespoon rice flour instead of all-purpose flour for a gluten-free kuku, and confirm the baking powder is labeled gluten-free.
Replace the barberries with unsweetened dried cranberries chopped to barberry size. Soak very dry cranberries in hot water for 5 minutes, drain and blot completely before folding them in.
Substitute up to 1 cup of the parsley or cilantro with baby spinach, but chop and squeeze the spinach dry so it does not dilute the eggs.
For a nut-free version, omit the walnuts and add 1/3 cup toasted pumpkin seeds; the flavor changes, but the garnish keeps a useful crunch.

A 9-inch square metal baking pan can replace the skillet. Oil it with all 3 tablespoons, preheat it in the oven for 5 minutes, carefully add the mixture and bake 22 to 27 minutes; it will make square portions without a stovetop-set crust.
storage: Cool leftover kuku within 2 hours, then refrigerate wedges in a shallow airtight container at 40°F or below for up to 4 days. Pack yogurt and vegetables separately. Reheat uncovered on a parchment-lined sheet pan at 325°F for 10 to 12 minutes, until the center reaches 165°F, or enjoy at room temperature after no more than 30 minutes out of the refrigerator. Freeze individually wrapped wedges for up to 2 months; thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat in the oven. Microwaving is safe but softens the crust, so use 50% power in 30-second bursts only when speed matters.
notes: Kuku sabzi is an herb-first Iranian egg dish, not a conventional vegetable frittata. The unusually high herb-to-egg ratio is intentional and gives the cut wedge its dark-green, almost leafy interior.

The CC0 photograph was independently verified on Wikimedia Commons: it depicts a triangular kuku sabzi wedge topped specifically with walnut halves and red barberries. Those toppings, the deep-green crumb and the wedge presentation all match this recipe and alt text.
The FDA lists 160°F as the safe minimum internal temperature for egg dishes. Check the center rather than an oily edge, then avoid overbaking once that temperature is reached.
Barberries can hide tiny stems or grit. Pick them over, rinse in a fine sieve and dry thoroughly; wet berries create gummy pockets in the egg mixture.
Calories and cost estimate one-sixth of the kuku, yogurt, flatbread and vegetables. Exact values vary with herb bunch size, walnut price and the bread served.

faqs.q: Why did my kuku sabzi turn watery or fall apart?
faqs.a: The herbs were probably wet, chopped into a paste or measured loosely. Spin and blot them dry, pulse only until finely chopped and pack five full cups before mixing. Also let the baked kuku rest 8 minutes so the egg structure firms before you invert and cut it.

faqs.q: Can I chop the herbs ahead of time?
faqs.a: Yes. Wash, dry and chop them up to 1 day ahead, then refrigerate in an airtight container lined with a dry towel. Mix them with the eggs only when the skillet and oven are ready; salted raw egg draws water from the herbs and should not wait on the counter.

faqs.q: Do I have to flip kuku sabzi on the stovetop?
faqs.a: No. Traditional versions may be cut or flipped to brown both sides, but the stovetop-to-oven method gives a stable browned base and a safely set 160°F center without maneuvering a heavy, herb-filled round. A final one- to two-minute broil adds color to the top while preserving clean wedges.
